claim: The comment says react-chatbot-kit ships as CommonJS. It says the kit's default import is the Chatbot component under webpack or Babel, and the whole module.exports object with Chatbot as a property under Vite or Node ESM. It also says importing `{ Chatbot }` by name fails under Node ESM because Node cannot see the kit's named exports.
verify_against: node_modules/react-chatbot-kit package.json (main/module/exports/type fields) and its build entry file
verify_hint: Open node_modules/react-chatbot-kit/package.json and the build entry it names. Check whether the build is CommonJS, whether it sets `__esModule` and `exports.default`, and how it assigns `Chatbot`, since a static `exports.Chatbot =` assignment is visible to Node's named-export detection.

claim: `(chatbotKit as { Chatbot?: typeof chatbotKit }).Chatbot ?? chatbotKit` resolves to the renderable Chatbot component in both cases: when the default import is the component itself, and when it is the module.exports object carrying a `Chatbot` property.

verify_hint: In the kit's build entry, check what `module.exports` / `exports.default` holds. Confirm that the object has a `Chatbot` key referencing the component, and that the component function has no `Chatbot` static that would be picked up instead.

claim: Once ChatWidget's layout effect sets mountedResetKeyRef to the new chatResetKey, the newly keyed react-chatbot-kit Chatbot has already constructed its ActionProvider with its setState. At that point controller.setState points at the mounted Chatbot, not at the unmounted previous one, so `controller.addMessages` in appendBlocks reaches the visible transcript.
verify_against: react-chatbot-kit Chatbot/Chat component source in node_modules/react-chatbot-kit (where it instantiates actionProvider); createKitAdapters and ChatController.bind in src/chat/ChatController.ts

Compare that with the ChatWidget useLayoutEffect at lines 485-487. Child layout effects run before the parent's, but a passive effect in the kit would run after the parent's layout effect.

claim: mount()'s appendBlocks, like the other handle methods, queues calls made before React attaches the ref and replays them in call order with other queued calls such as open(). A replayed appendBlocks that follows a replayed open() in the same flush still shows its blocks.
verify_against: withHandle in src/mount.tsx; appendBlocks and hasOpenedRef in src/widget/ChatWidget.tsx
verify_hint: Trace `const w = mount(el, opts); w.open(); w.appendBlocks([...])` through withHandle's queue flush and the hasOpenedRef layout effect
evidence: src/mount.tsx:56 appendBlocks goes through withHandle (33-47), which pushes onto the shared `queued` array when ref.current is unset and flushes in push order (splice(0).forEach, line 44), so it is replayed in call order with open(). In the flush, open() calls setOpen(true), which calls setHasOpened(true) (ChatWidget.tsx:167-177). These updates are batched and no re-render has happened, so hasOpenedRef.current (454-457) is still false when the next queued appendBlocks runs. appendBlocks then takes the else branch (465-466) and buffers into initialMessages via setInitialMessages. The same batched render sets hasOpened true and the new initialMessages. chatConfig is memoised on initialMessages (503-504), and the Chatbot mounts only when hasOpened is true (572). It therefore mounts seeded with the appended blocks, so they show. If the widget was already opened, hasOpenedRef is true and controller.addMessages is used directly. Not run at runtime. I did not read how the Chatbot kit consumes initialMessages at mount, so that step rests on the memoised config and the mount gating.
